hook.text: In 1996, Dolly the sheep became the first mammal cloned from an adult cell.

buildup.text: Scientists took a cell from one sheep's udder and transferred its nucleus into an empty egg.

discovery.text: The egg developed into a lamb genetically identical to the donor—a true clone.

twist.text: Dolly aged faster than normal and developed arthritis. Cloning isn't a perfect copy after all.

climax.text: Today, cloning is used in agriculture and research, but human cloning remains banned worldwide.

punchline.text: Same DNA, but never quite the same animal.

quiz.question: What was Dolly the sheep famous for?
options: First mammal cloned from an adult cell

details.summary: Cloning produces genetically identical copies of an organism. Dolly the sheep, born in 1996, was the first mammal cloned from an adult cell using somatic cell nuclear transfer, proving that differentiated cells retain their full genetic potential.
details.whyItMatters: Cloning demonstrated that cell specialization is reversible and opened the door to stem cell research and regenerative medicine. It also raised profound ethical debates about reproductive cloning in humans.
takeaways: Dolly was cloned by transferring an adult cell nucleus into an empty egg
Cloning proves differentiated cells contain the complete genome
Cloned animals often show premature aging and health problems

faq.question: Why was Dolly the sheep so important scientifically?
faq.answer: Dolly proved that a mature, specialized cell could be reprogrammed to create an entire organism. This overturned the belief that differentiation was irreversible and opened research avenues in stem cells and regenerative medicine.

faq.question: Why is human reproductive cloning considered unethical?
faq.answer: Animal cloning has extremely high failure rates and cloned animals frequently suffer health problems. Attempting human cloning with current technology would require many failed embryos and likely produce children with serious medical issues.
